scenes.text: On the fourteenth of October 2026, Portugal's cabinet announced who would run its national airline.
The winner was Lufthansa, and the price was 1.025 billion euros for 44.9 percent of TAP, a sum that climbs to about 1.2 billion euros if the share reserved for employees is counted.
Here is the strange part.
TAP lost 99.2 million euros in the first half of this year, 40 percent more than a year earlier.
It flies out of a home airport with a single runway, squeezed in among the neighborhoods of the capital.
And the buyer will not even own a majority.
Yet Lufthansa beat Air France-KLM to get it, and Portugal agreed to let the German group take over day to day management.
So why would one of the biggest airline groups in Europe pay over a billion euros for this?
The answer is the title of this video.
Lisbon is about to become Lufthansa's next fortress hub, and almost every number says it should not work.
This is the story of a mid-sized airline, a crowded airport, and the most valuable stretch of map in southern Europe.
Start with the airline.
TAP was founded on the fourteenth of March 1945, and its first aircraft were a pair of Douglas DC-3s.
Its first commercial flight, in 1946, went from Lisbon to Madrid.
In 1960 it began crossing the Atlantic to Rio de Janeiro, and in 1967 it became the first airline in Europe to operate only jets.
It joined Star Alliance in 2005.
Then came the roller coaster.
In 2015 the government sold a majority to a private consortium led by David Neeleman, the founder of JetBlue and Azul.
The state later took control back, and the pandemic forced a rescue that came with a strict restructuring plan.
Brussels has since acknowledged that those measures were carried out and that TAP's long-term viability is restored.
Today TAP flies 101 aircraft to 93 destinations.
In 2025 it carried 16.7 million passengers, and 84.2 percent of its seats were full.
Revenue reached 4.3 billion euros, but the net profit was only 4.1 million euros, down from 53.7 million the year before.
That was its fourth profitable year in a row.
The drop came from a one-off tax charge of 42 million euros, and without it TAP says the profit would have been about 46 million.
The maintenance business helped too, with revenue up 10.7 percent.
So this is not a broken airline.
It is a thin-margin airline that has climbed back from the edge.
Now the airport.
Humberto Delgado handled 36.1 million passengers in 2025, up 2.9 percent in a year, and it does all of that on one runway.
In 2023 it handled 33.6 million, roughly double what it handled a decade before.
Across the whole country, Portugal's airports set a record of 72.5 million passengers in 2025, up 4.7 percent.
Lisbon carries half of that on its own, and Faro, the gateway to the Algarve, adds about 10 million more.
Tourism is booming, and the capital's airport is full.
So what makes Lisbon worth fighting for?
Geography and language.
Lisbon sits on the western edge of the continent, a natural jumping-off point for the Atlantic.
Of TAP's 93 destinations, 52 are in Europe, 16 are in South and Central America, 14 are in Africa and 11 are in North America.
That mix is the whole logic of a hub.
Short flights gather passengers from across Europe, and long flights carry them over the ocean.
Brazil is the crown jewel.
TAP's network there is growing to 15 destinations, and 10 of them are served only by TAP.

Add Portuguese-speaking Africa, and you get what Reuters called the main attraction of the airline: valuable landing slots linking Lisbon with Brazil, Africa and the United States, backed by a diaspora that keeps the planes full.
Now think about what a fortress hub is.
It is an airport where one airline controls most of the flights and most of the connections.
Rivals struggle to get slots, and the home airline can feed its long flights with its own short ones.
Lufthansa already runs fortress hubs in Frankfurt, Munich, Zurich and Vienna, and each one is a machine for moving passengers between continents.
Lisbon would add a very different machine.
Instead of Asia and the North Atlantic, its strength is the South Atlantic, plus a growing set of routes to the United States.
That is a map Lufthansa cannot easily build from scratch, because the slots, the traffic rights and the language ties took TAP decades to collect.
That is why three airline groups raised their hands.
In November 2025, Air France-KLM, Lufthansa and IAG all declared their interest.
Air France-KLM promised to make Lisbon its only hub in southern Europe, linking the Americas and Africa.
Lufthansa called TAP a strong airline and a leading carrier on South Atlantic routes, with a long history as a Star Alliance partner.
IAG, the owner of Iberia, dropped out in April, saying it needed a clear path to full ownership.
In other words, Iberia's owner walked away from the airline next door.
That left two bidders and a long fight.
Binding offers followed in the summer, improved offers arrived in late September, and the cabinet chose Lufthansa on the fourteenth of October.
But there is a catch hiding in that number.
Lufthansa is paying for 44.9 percent of TAP, not for control.
Portugal keeps 50.1 percent, and another 5 percent is offered first to TAP's own employees at the same price.
If staff do not take it up, Lufthansa buys it, and that is how the bill grows toward 1.2 billion euros.
Yet it will run the airline day to day.
The privatization decree even allows the state to sell the remaining stake to the same buyer later.
And Portugal set conditions.
The buyer must keep serving Lisbon, Porto, Faro, the Azores and Madeira, and Lufthansa has promised to preserve the airline's national identity and to grow the fleet.
The deal also still has to clear regulators.
So Lufthansa is buying influence first and ownership later.
Then the story flips.
Look at that first half loss again.
99.2 million euros sounds terrible, but the first half is the weak season for an airline that lives on summer tourists and holiday travel to Brazil.
In 2025, TAP lost money in the first six months, then earned 126 million euros in the third quarter alone and wiped out the damage.
And passengers are not leaving.
TAP carried a record 8.2 million passengers in the first half of this year, up 4.2 percent, with operating revenue up 4.3 percent.
The airline is seasonal, not sinking.
The numbers say the opposite of what the headline loss suggests.
Net debt stood at 2.6 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization at the end of 2025.
That is a manageable level for an airline that was in rescue mode only a few years ago.
Capacity grew 3.1 percent in 2025, while passenger traffic measured in kilometers grew 5.5 percent, so planes were fuller, not just more numerous.
And TAP wants to grow outside the capital too, with new routes from Porto and a new maintenance hub there.
Those are not the numbers of a rescue case.
They are the numbers of a small airline that the pandemic bent but did not break, and that a bigger group can now feed with more connections.
There is one more detail worth a pause, and it is about a name.
The airport carries the name of Humberto Delgado, the air force officer who created TAP in 1945.
Locals still call it Portela.
Both names may not last.
The government's plan is to build a new airport at Alcochete, on the far side of the Tagus river, name it after the poet Luís de Camões, and one day dismantle the old one.
So the airline that an officer founded may one day outlive the airport that carries his name.
Eighty years after a DC-3 flew to Madrid with the first paying passengers, TAP's whole future depends on where the runway will be.
Here is what could break it.
The real bottleneck is not the airline.
It is the runway.
Lisbon already handles 36.1 million passengers on one strip of tarmac, and the government expects 39 million by 2030.
Planned upgrades should lift the airport from 38 to 45 movements an hour, but that is a patch, not a cure.

The new airport is expected to cost close to 9 billion euros, it will need a third bridge across the Tagus to be useful, and estimates for its opening point to the middle of the 2030s at the earliest.
Portugal says Lufthansa has committed to growing the fleet.
More planes are coming, and the runway they will use is the same one.
There is a second risk, and it sits in Frankfurt, not Lisbon.
Analysts quoted by Reuters point out that Lufthansa's own mainline airline is still losing money.
The group is also still digesting ITA Airways, the Italian flag carrier, on top of Swiss and Austrian.
Every airline it buys needs money, management and attention at the same time.
If Lufthansa spreads itself too thin, Lisbon could become one more project on a very long list.
And there is a third risk, which is political.
A state that keeps 50.1 percent of an airline will always have opinions about routes, jobs and fares, and those opinions do not always match the plans of a German owner.
So what should you watch next?
Four things.
First, the regulators, because a deal this size will be examined closely.
Second, the employee share, which decides how much Lufthansa ends up owning on day one.
Third, the schedule, because the first new routes will show which markets Lufthansa believes in.
And fourth, the runway, because no amount of money can add flights to a strip of tarmac that is already full.
So what is Lisbon really?
It is not Europe's biggest airport, and TAP is not Europe's richest airline.
Lisbon is a small hub with a big map.
It has Brazil, Africa and North America in one network, a language and a diaspora that keep the planes full, and now the backing of a group that already owns Swiss, Austrian and ITA.
Its weaknesses are just as clear: one runway, thin profits and a deal that is not yet closed.
If Lufthansa can feed Lisbon faster than the runway fills up, the hub works.
If not, it will be a billion euro lesson in geography.
Either way, the message is clear.
One of Europe's last flag carriers without a big airline group behind it has chosen its side.
Against all logic, Lisbon is about to become Lufthansa's next fortress hub.
